terms.grammar: phrase: litotes with mediōcris (also haud mediōcris)
evidence: Caes. BG 3.20: nōn mediōcrem sibi dīligentiam adhibendam intellegēbat
Cic. Rep. 2.55: haud mediōcris hic … vir fuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin praises by denying the opposite: “not middling” is “considerable, remarkable” (Lewis & Short, s.v. mediōcris). Significantly, considerably: nōn mediōcriter (Caes. BG 1.39, Lewis & Short).
What stands out, as if marked.

terms.grammar: adjective; mostly the neuter with a genitive
terms.comment: Between much and little (Lewis & Short): aliquantum agrī, a fair piece of land.

evidence: Quint. 9.2.44: dīlūcida et significāns dēscrīptiō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A term of rhetoric for a word or a description that conveys its meaning well (Quintilian); it does not mean “considerable”.

phrases.latin: nōn mediōcrem sibi dīligentiam adhibendam intellegēbat
phrases.english: he understood that he would have to take no small care

phrases.latin: quālis vidētur opera tibi vōcis meae? — īnsignis, inquit, sīc ut, nisi nōssem tuum animum genusque, similī fūgissem metū
phrases.english: ‘How do you like what my voice did?’ ‘Remarkable,’ he said, ‘so much so that, had I not known your nature and your breed, I would have run away in fear like the rest.’

sources: Lewis & Short: mediocris · Lewis & Short: insignis · Lewis & Short: aliquantus · Lewis & Short: significo
